title: Old English & Beowulf
description: Anglo-Saxon poetry, alliterative verse, the heroic age

concepts.title: Old English
concepts.contentHtml:
Old English (Anglo-Saxon) was spoken in England from roughly 450 to 1100 CE. Its surviving literature is small — perhaps 30,000 lines of verse total — but distinctive.

The major surviving poems: Beowulf, The Wanderer, The Seafarer, The Dream of the Rood, The Battle of Maldon. Plus religious works (Cædmon's hymn, Cynewulf's poems).

Most survives in four manuscripts. The Exeter Book (c. 970) contains most of the lyric poetry; the Beowulf manuscript (c. 1000) preserves the epic.

concepts.title: Alliterative Verse
concepts.contentHtml:
Old English poetry uses alliterative verse, not rhyme. Each line has four stressed syllables divided by a caesura (pause) into two half-lines. Three of the four stresses must alliterate.

Example: 'Hwæt! We Gardena || in geardagum, / þeodcyninga, || þrym gefrunon...'

The line system gives Old English verse its distinctive sound — heavy, rhythmic, packed with consonants. The form survived past the Norman Conquest in works like Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (c. 1400).

Modern poets including Tolkien (a professional Anglo-Saxonist) and Seamus Heaney revived alliterative verse. Heaney's 1999 Beowulf translation is now standard.

concepts.title: Beowulf
concepts.contentHtml:
Beowulf is a 3,182-line epic in Old English, probably composed 700-1000 CE. Set in 6th-century Scandinavia. The hero Beowulf, a Geat warrior, kills the monster Grendel, then Grendel's mother, then dies fighting a dragon fifty years later.

The poem combines pagan heroic ethos with Christian framing. Beowulf is a pre-Christian hero treated by a Christian poet — the result is a sustained meditation on mortality, fame, and the limits of heroic achievement.

Key passages: Beowulf's underwater fight with Grendel's mother; the dragon hoard; Beowulf's funeral pyre and the woman's lament at the close. Tolkien wrote his most famous critical essay on it, 'The Monsters and the Critics,' 1936.

concepts.title: Elegies and Lyrics
concepts.contentHtml:
Old English produced major short poems alongside Beowulf.

The Wanderer: a former retainer, alone after his lord's death, meditates on transience. 'Where now the horse and rider? Where now the giver of treasure?'

The Seafarer: a sea-voyager's hardship and longing fused with religious ascent.

The Dream of the Rood: the cross of the Crucifixion narrates the event from its own perspective.

The Wife's Lament and Wulf and Eadwacer: rare female-voiced poems of separation and grief.

The Battle of Maldon: an account of an actual 991 battle, ending with the famous line about loyalty after defeat.

concepts.title: After 1066
concepts.contentHtml:
The Norman Conquest of 1066 ended Old English as a literary language. French became the language of court and administration; Latin remained the language of learning. English continued as a vernacular spoken language but largely disappeared from elite writing for two centuries.

When English re-emerged in the 14th century — in Chaucer, Langland, the Gawain-poet — it was a transformed language (Middle English), with massive French and Latin vocabulary additions. Old English looks more foreign to a modern reader than Middle English does.

What survives of Anglo-Saxon literary culture is mainly through these poems. They preserve a worldview — heroic, fatalistic, intensely loyal — that the post-1066 tradition would not quite reproduce.

title: Chaucer & Middle English
description: The Canterbury Tales — the vernacular finds its voice

concepts.title: Middle English
concepts.contentHtml:
Middle English (roughly 1100-1500) was spoken England's transformed post-Conquest tongue. By the late 14th century it had stabilised enough to produce major literary works.

Major Middle English works: The Canterbury Tales, Piers Plowman, Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, The Book of Margery Kempe, the medieval drama cycles (York, Chester, Wakefield).

The London dialect of Chaucer became the basis of standard modern English.

concepts.title: Chaucer
concepts.contentHtml:
Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343-1400) was the central figure of late medieval English literature. Civil servant, diplomat, customs official, and finally Clerk of the King's Works — he wrote in his spare time.

Major works: The Book of the Duchess (1370s), Troilus and Criseyde (1380s), The Legend of Good Women, and the unfinished Canterbury Tales (begun late 1380s).

His distinctive achievement: making English a major literary language. Earlier English works existed; Chaucer's combined sustained narrative skill, psychological depth, comic range, and stylistic flexibility at a level that established the language as adequate to serious literary work.

concepts.title: The Canterbury Tales
concepts.contentHtml:
The Canterbury Tales is a frame narrative. Twenty-nine pilgrims travelling to Canterbury agree to tell tales along the way — two each on the journey out, two on the return. The full plan would have produced 120 tales. Chaucer completed about 24.

The pilgrims represent medieval English society — Knight, Miller, Wife of Bath, Pardoner, Franklin, Prioress, Reeve, and many others. Their tales are sometimes appropriate to their tellers (the Knight's romance), sometimes ironic against them (the Pardoner's anti-greed sermon from a corrupt cleric).

The Wife of Bath, in particular, is one of literature's first fully realised female characters — speaking from her own complex perspective, defending female experience, undermining clerical anti-feminism.

concepts.title: Other 14th-Century Works
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond Chaucer:

William Langland's Piers Plowman (c. 1370-90), an alliterative-verse vision poem about religious and social reform.

The Gawain-poet (anonymous, c. 1380): four poems in West Midlands dialect, including Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. The great Arthurian poem in English, fusing romance and Christian moral testing.

Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love (c. 1395): the first known book in English by a woman. Visionary, theologically subtle.

Margery Kempe's Book (1430s): the first English autobiography. A pilgrimage record by a non-aristocratic married woman.

concepts.title: Reading Middle English
concepts.contentHtml:
Middle English looks foreign on first encounter but is closer to modern English than Old English. With ten minutes' practice and footnotes, most modern readers can follow Chaucer in the original.

Lines from the General Prologue: 'Whan that Aprill, with his shoures soote / The droghte of March hath perced to the roote, / And bathed every veyne in swich licour, / Of which vertu engendred is the flour...'

Key features: vowels pronounced (the final 'e' in many words), spelling not yet standardised, French and Latin loanwords flooding in, grammatical inflections still active.

Reading Middle English directly rewards the small effort. Modernised translations lose much of Chaucer's music.

title: Dante & the Italian Renaissance
description: The Divine Comedy, Petrarch, the sonnet's birth

concepts.title: Dante
concepts.contentHtml:
Dante Alighieri (1265-1321) is the central figure of medieval European literature. His Commedia (later called Divina Commedia, the Divine Comedy) is a 14,233-line epic in three parts: Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso. Composed roughly 1308-1320.

The poem is a vision of the afterlife. The narrator (called Dante) journeys through Hell guided by Virgil, then Purgatory, then Heaven guided by his beloved Beatrice.

Dante wrote in Italian (specifically Tuscan) when serious poetry was conventionally Latin. The choice helped establish Italian as a major literary language.

concepts.title: The Divine Comedy in Detail
concepts.contentHtml:
Inferno (Hell) is the most-read of the three. The damned are arranged by sin, descending — the lustful in upper hell, the betrayers (worst) at the bottom, where Satan is encased in ice. Memorable figures: Paolo and Francesca; Farinata; Ulysses; Count Ugolino.

Purgatorio (Purgatory) is more redemptive. Souls climb a mountain through seven terraces (one per deadly sin), purifying themselves.

Paradiso (Heaven) is theologically and poetically the most ambitious. Dante ascends through the nine spheres to direct vision of God.

The whole poem is in terza rima — interlocking three-line rhymed stanzas Dante invented.

concepts.title: Petrarch and the Sonnet
concepts.contentHtml:
Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch, 1304-1374) was the next major Italian poet. His Canzoniere ('Song Book') collects 366 poems, mostly sonnets, mostly addressed to Laura — a real woman he saw once, perhaps, in 1327, and never spoke to.

The sequence invented the European love-poetry tradition. The lover's longing for an idealised, unattainable beloved; the lover's self-analysis under the lash of unrequited love; the play of presence and absence.

Petrarch also gave the Petrarchan sonnet its definitive shape — 14 lines divided 8/6 (octave + sestet) with a turn between them.

concepts.title: Boccaccio and Prose
concepts.contentHtml:
Giovanni Boccaccio (1313-1375) was the third of the great Italian Trecento writers. His Decameron (1349-53) is a frame narrative — ten young Florentines fleeing the Black Death tell ten stories each over ten days.

Range: comic, tragic, romantic, bawdy, satirical. The book defends pleasure, mocks clerical hypocrisy, celebrates wit and resourcefulness — a Renaissance outlook in prose form.

The Decameron's frame structure influenced Chaucer (who knew Boccaccio's work) and the European prose tradition broadly.

concepts.title: The Italian Renaissance
concepts.contentHtml:
The 15th and 16th centuries continued Italian literary leadership. Lorenzo de' Medici's circle in Florence; Pico della Mirandola's philosophical writings; Marsilio Ficino's revival of Platonic philosophy; Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando Furioso (1516); Torquato Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata (1581).

Niccolò Machiavelli's The Prince (1513) is more political treatise than literature, but its influence on European prose was enormous.

Italian Renaissance writing — its sonnet tradition, its prose forms, its treatment of love and politics — provided the European context against which English Renaissance writers (Wyatt, Sidney, Spenser, Shakespeare) would define their work.

title: Northern Renaissance
description: Erasmus, More, Rabelais — humanism reshapes the page

concepts.title: Humanism
concepts.contentHtml:
Renaissance humanism — the recovery and study of classical Greek and Roman texts — moved north from Italy in the late 15th and 16th centuries. Northern humanists like Erasmus, More, and Rabelais combined Italian textual scholarship with their own distinctive concerns.

The shared programme: read the ancients in their own languages; recover the original meaning of biblical and classical texts; apply that learning to current religious and political life.

The printing press (Gutenberg, 1450s) accelerated the project.

concepts.title: Erasmus
concepts.contentHtml:
Desiderius Erasmus (c. 1466-1536) was the central Northern humanist. Dutch by birth, he wrote in Latin, lived in England, France, the Netherlands, Switzerland.

His major works: The Praise of Folly (1509), a satirical mock-encomium delivered by Folly herself; the Adages; the Greek New Testament (1516), the first printed Greek edition, foundation for the Reformation translations.

Erasmus's distinctive position: he wanted reform of the Catholic Church without breaking with it. Luther and the Protestants pushed past him; the Catholic Counter-Reformation suspected him.

concepts.title: Thomas More
concepts.contentHtml:
Sir Thomas More (1478-1535) was Erasmus's English counterpart. Friend of Erasmus, lawyer, statesman, eventually Chancellor under Henry VIII, eventually executed for refusing to recognise Henry's break with Rome.

His Utopia (1516) — written in Latin — invented the modern utopian fiction genre. The book describes an imaginary island commonwealth: communal property, religious tolerance, six-hour workdays, no money, planned cities.

How seriously More meant the ideal society as a programme is debated. Some elements (slavery, war) make Utopia less utopian than the modern reader expects.

concepts.title: Rabelais
concepts.contentHtml:
François Rabelais (c. 1483-1553) was the great French humanist comedian. His five books of Gargantua and Pantagruel (1532-64) follow two giant kings through wildly inventive adventures.

The mode: erudite, scatological, parodic, violently anti-clerical, encyclopedic. Rabelais piles up lists, neologisms, multilingual puns, classical allusions, and crude jokes in proportions found nowhere else.

Mikhail Bakhtin's Rabelais and His World (1965) made Rabelais central to literary theory. Bakhtin coined the term carnivalesque for the festival mode Rabelais inhabits — official hierarchies inverted, the body celebrated, polyphonic voices contending.

concepts.title: Montaigne and the Essay
concepts.contentHtml:
Michel de Montaigne (1533-1592) invented the modern essay. His three books of Essais (1580, 1588, 1595 posthumous) gave Europe a new form: the personal, exploratory, self-questioning prose meditation.

Topics: cannibals, friendship, books, fear, drunkenness, his own kidney stones. The essays digress, contradict themselves, revisit earlier points.

The essay as Montaigne invented it has been one of the most generative literary forms. Bacon, Hazlitt, Emerson, Woolf, Orwell, Sontag, Maggie Nelson — all work in his shadow.

Montaigne also marks the end of the Renaissance and the beginning of the modern: a writer not preaching certainty but exploring the difficulty of knowing.

title: Cervantes & Don Quixote
description: The first modern novel and the end of chivalry

concepts.title: Cervantes
concepts.contentHtml:
Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547-1616) had one of the most eventful biographies of any major writer. Soldier wounded at the Battle of Lepanto (1571); captured by Algerian pirates and held for five years until ransomed; struggling tax collector; brief imprisonment for accounting irregularities; finally success at 58 with Part 1 of Don Quixote (1605).

Part 2 followed in 1615. He died in 1616, the same year as Shakespeare.

Cervantes wrote prolifically — plays, poems, the Exemplary Novels, the late Persiles y Sigismunda. Don Quixote dwarfs the rest in importance.

concepts.title: The Premise
concepts.contentHtml:
Alonso Quixano, an aging gentleman from La Mancha, has read too many medieval chivalric romances. He decides to become a knight-errant. He renames himself Don Quixote, finds a peasant named Sancho Panza for a 'squire,' and sets out to right wrongs and rescue ladies.

The famous early scene: Quixote sees windmills as giants and charges them. Sancho tries to convince him they're windmills. Quixote insists; charges; is unhorsed by a sail. He attributes his defeat to enchantment.

The premise is parody. By 1605 chivalric romances were considered absurd. What makes the book transcend parody: the depth of the two main characters and the philosophical seriousness Cervantes finds in his idealistic madman.

concepts.title: Why Don Quixote Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
By common consent, Don Quixote is where the modern novel begins.

It treats characters as more than types. Quixote is funny but also heroic, mad but morally serious. Sancho starts as comic foil and becomes one of literature's great companions.

It plays with metafiction. Part 2 (1615) takes account of the published Part 1 — the characters know they've been written about, encounter readers of their earlier adventures, react to a fraudulent unauthorised sequel that had appeared.

It opens the realist mode. Quixote's idealism is constantly checked against grubby actual reality.

concepts.title: Influence
concepts.contentHtml:
Subsequent fiction is hard to imagine without Cervantes.

The 18th-century English novel (Fielding, Sterne) drew on him directly. Tristram Shandy's metafictional play descends from Part 2 of Quixote.

Flaubert's Madame Bovary is a Quixote-female-version: Emma's romantic novels lead her astray as Quixote's chivalric ones did.

Latin American magical realism — Borges, García Márquez, Cortázar — claims direct descent. Borges's 'Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote' (1939) is a metafictional masterpiece.

The phrase 'tilting at windmills' has entered every European language.

concepts.title: Reading Don Quixote
concepts.contentHtml:
The book is long — 1,000 pages — and uneven. Some episodes drag, particularly inserted novellas in Part 1.

But the major scenes are extraordinary. Quixote's vigil to be knighted at the inn. The freeing of the galley slaves. The cave of Montesinos. The encounter with the duke and duchess in Part 2 who manipulate Quixote for their entertainment. Quixote's final return home, recovery of sanity, and death — perhaps the most moving deathbed scene in fiction.

Edith Grossman's 2003 English translation is the modern standard. John Rutherford's 2000 Penguin translation is also widely respected.

The book is funnier than its reputation. It's also sadder. Both moods coexist throughout.
